core: Fixed vs variable costs and total cost (TC = FC + VC) in the short run
Average fixed cost (AFC), average variable cost (AVC), and average total cost (ATC)
Marginal cost (MC = change in TC / change in Q)
The typical U-shape of the ATC curve and the fact that MC crosses AVC and ATC at their minimum points
Economies and diseconomies of scale on the long-run average cost (LRAC) curve
supporting: One-sentence link: diminishing marginal returns is why marginal cost eventually rises
LRAC as the lower envelope of short-run ATC curves
outOfScope: The physical production function, marginal product, and average product (owned by economics:foundations:production)
How a firm chooses profit-maximizing output where MC = MR (perfect-competition, monopoly)
Explicit vs implicit costs and accounting vs economic profit beyond a brief mention

claims.claim: In the short run a firm's total cost splits into fixed costs, which do not change with the level of output, and variable costs, which rise and fall with output; TC = FC + VC.

Marginal cost is the change in total cost divided by the change in output (MC = ΔTC/ΔQ) and is generally upward-sloping because diminishing marginal returns make additional units more costly to produce.
Average total cost is total cost divided by quantity (ATC = TC/Q); average variable cost is VC/Q and average fixed cost is FC/Q; and AFC + AVC = ATC.
Average fixed cost falls continuously as output rises because a fixed total is spread over more units.

The average total cost curve is typically U-shaped: it starts high because fixed cost dominates at low output, falls as fixed cost spreads out, then rises as diminishing returns push variable costs up faster.

The marginal cost curve intersects the average variable cost and average total cost curves at their minimum points, because MC below the average pulls the average down and MC above the average pulls it up.

In the long run all inputs are variable, so a firm can choose its scale; the long-run average cost curve shows the lowest cost of producing each quantity and is the lower envelope of the short-run ATC curves.

Economies of scale exist where per-unit cost falls as output rises (OpenStax alarm-clock example: 1,000 clocks at $12 each in a small plant vs 5,000 clocks at $4 each in a large plant); constant returns to scale leave average cost roughly flat; diseconomies of scale raise average cost as the firm grows too large to manage.
